title: Measure the Earth with a shadow
hook: Over 2,000 years ago someone sized the whole planet with a stick and a walk. How?

knows: that a full circle is 360 degrees
doesNotKnow: how the size of the Earth was first measured
that a shadow angle and one distance are enough

misconception: The size of the Earth could only be found after satellites or long voyages.
objective: The learner can explain that, with parallel sunlight, the shadow angle equals the angle at the Earth's centre, so circumference = (360 / angle) x distance.

claims.text: In the account, at noon on the solstice a well at Syene had no shadow, a pole's shadow in Alexandria made 7.2 degrees, and the distance was 5,000 stadia, giving 250,000 stadia.
claims.source: Cleomedes, 'On the Circular Motions of the Celestial Bodies' (I.7), reporting Eratosthenes, whose own text is lost. The often-quoted 252,000 stadia comes from other ancient writers (e.g. Strabo, Pliny). From memory, not checked online. The lesson says 'as the account tells it'.

claims.text: Because the Sun is so far away its rays arrive parallel, so the shadow angle equals the angle at the Earth's centre between the two places.
claims.source: Alternate angles between parallel lines (the rays) cut by a transversal (the radius through Alexandria). The Sun's rays across Earth's diameter diverge by under 0.01 degrees (12,742 km / 150 million km), which is negligible here.

claims.text: With modern numbers, 7.11 degrees and 843 km give 50.6 arcs and 42,684 km, within 7% of the true 40,008 km.
claims.source: Latitudes Alexandria 31.20 N 29.92 E and Aswan 24.09 N 32.90 E (gazetteer, from memory, not checked online); difference 7.11 degrees; great-circle distance 843.2 km by geoDistance with R = 6,371.0088 km, computed in Demo.tsx; 843 x 360 / 7.11 = 42,684 km, which the stage's Seen line and the reveal both show as 42,684 km (the circumference readout's rounding); 360 / 7.11 = 50.6 at the arcs readout's one decimal. 40,008 km is the WGS84 meridional circumference (about 40,007.86 km, from memory). The cities are not on one meridian (3 degrees of longitude apart), which accounts for much of the excess. | FC pass 26 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Coordinates checked against GeoNames (npm cities.json, GeoNames gazetteer extract, opened locally): Alexandria 31.20176 N 29.91582 E, Aswan 24.09082 N 32.89942 E, which round to the lesson's 31.20/29.92 and 24.09/32.90. 40,008 km: GeographicLib (npm geographiclib-geodesic) WGS84 a = 6378137 m, f = 1/298.257223563, 4 x geodesic(0,0 -> 90,0) = 40,007.86 km. Own node with d3-geo geoDistance and R = 6,371.0088: 7.11 degrees, 843.2 km (843), 360/7.11 = 50.6, 843 x 360/7.11 = 42,684 km, 6.7% over (prints 7%). With unrounded GeoNames coordinates the circumference is 42,700 km, still within 7%.

claims.text: Nobody knows the exact length of a stadion, so how close Eratosthenes was in km cannot be said.
claims.source: Proposed stadion lengths range from about 157 m to about 185 m (e.g. Engels 1985, 'The Length of Eratosthenes' Stade', American Journal of Philology; from memory, not checked online).

claims.text: In the account, the Sun stood straight overhead at Syene at noon on the summer solstice, so the well had no shadow.
claims.source: A vertical well shows no shadow on its sides only when the Sun is at the zenith (rays parallel to the well's axis). This is the reading of the account in Cleomedes I.7; Syene is in fact about 0.65 degrees north of the Tropic of Cancer (brief caveat 4), so the 'as the account tells it' framing applies. Stage label: 'Syene: Sun overhead, no shadow'. | FC pass 26 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): DISPUTED. The derivation (no shadow down a vertical well only with the Sun at the zenith) holds, but the sentence states as fact that the Sun was straight overhead at Syene. It was not quite: Syene is at 24.09 N (GeoNames), north of the Tropic of Cancer (about 0.65 degrees north today per the lesson's own brief caveat 4; still a few tenths of a degree in Eratosthenes' time). The brief asked for 'in the account' framing; the reveal sentence ('At Syene the Sun was straight overhead, so the well had no shadow.') and the stage label ('Syene: Sun overhead, no shadow') carry none, and the 'as the account tells it' phrase belongs to the next sentence. Fix (demo-builder): frame it as the account, e.g. 'In the account, the Sun stood straight overhead at Syene at noon on the summer solstice, so the well had no shadow.' Related: the question says 'At noon a well in Syene has no shadow' with no date; c1 has 'on the solstice'. | v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, W-249): reworded to the account framing the checker gave. Reveal: 'In the account, the Sun stood straight overhead at Syene at noon on the summer solstice, so the well had no shadow.' Stage label (two lines): 'Syene, in the account:' / 'Sun overhead, no shadow'. Question now opens 'In the account, at noon on the summer solstice a well in Syene has no shadow; ...' (covered by c1). The lesson makes no modern claim that the Sun was exactly overhead. Needs re-check. | FC pass 27 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): HELD UNVERIFIED (not disputed). Stage part checked: the reveal string matches the claim word for word, the Syene label is two lines 'Syene, in the account:' / 'Sun overhead, no shadow', and the question opens 'In the account, at noon on the summer solstice'. No modern claim of an overhead Sun remains, and the derivation half (no shadow down a vertical well only with the Sun at the zenith) holds. But what the sentence now asserts is what the account says (Sun overhead, at noon, on the summer solstice, a well). That cannot be derived; it rests on Cleomedes I.7 (and, for the well, possibly Strabo or Pliny rather than Cleomedes), and none of these could be opened (proxy 403 / DNS failure on penelope.uchicago.edu, perseus.tufts.edu, wikipedia, mathshistory, goobi.tib.eu). Search snippets only. Independence: this wording was drafted by the fact-checker in pass 26, so a fact-checker should not be the one to self-confirm it from snippets either. Needs an openable source or an evaluation-steward ruling (board).

recall.question: Two towns 1,000 km apart lie on one north-south line. At the same noon their shadows differ by 9 degrees. How big is the planet round?
recall.why: The shadow difference is the angle at the centre. 9 degrees is 1/40 of 360, so the circumference is 40 x 1,000 km = 40,000 km.
